story: Dovre National Park is a link. It lies between Rondane National Park to the south-east and Dovrefjell-Sunndalsfjella to the north, and with the landscape protection areas around it, it joins them into an almost continuous protected area running from the Sunndal mountains to Ringebufjellet. Its main purpose is to safeguard the range of the Rondane wild reindeer herd. Almost all of the park lies above the tree line, on plateaus and rounded summits between 1,200 and 1,600 metres; the highest point, Storhøe, reaches 1,716 metres.

The landscape was shaped by the melting of the last ice sheet: meltwater channels, kettle holes where dead ice lay, and eskers. Around the highest summits it is almost arctic, with traces of permafrost, and the park holds some of the southernmost palsa mires in Norway. The bedrock includes greenstone and black phyllite, which weather into rich soil. That makes Dovre a core area for Norwegian mountain plants, among them rarities such as the Dovre poppy and the Dovre dandelion.

Wild reindeer have roamed these mountains for more than 10,000 years, and the herd here is among the last of Europe's original wild mountain reindeer. They are easily disturbed. A vulnerable population of wolverine lives in the area, and their tracks are a common sight; birds of prey hunt over the plateaus, and the open fells are home to the dotterel, the shore lark, the golden eagle and the gyrfalcon.

People have hunted reindeer here since prehistory, and the park is a core area for the remains: whole trapping systems with guiding fences, stone-lined and earth-dug pits, bow emplacements and stone shelters. The great seasonal migration that fed the trappers is gone, its range split into smaller, isolated pieces by development and traffic. From the Middle Ages the route over Dovre was a well-known — and feared — road between Oslo and Nidaros, travelled in the Middle Ages by pilgrims to St Olav's shrine and known both as Pilegrimsleden and as Kongevegen, the King's Road; the pilgrim path, marked again in 1997, crosses the westernmost part of the park. The park was created on 24 October 2003.
howItWorks: The right to roam, allemannsretten, applies: you may walk anywhere in the outfield, camp for two nights in one place without asking — longer high in the mountains — at least 150 metres from a house or cabin, and pick berries and mushrooms. The regulation allows careful use of wood for campfires, though there is little wood above the tree line. From 15 April to 15 September it is forbidden across Norway to light a fire in or near forest and other open country unless the municipality has allowed it or a fire plainly cannot spread; check with Dovre or Folldal municipality before you go. A tent may stay more than a week in one place only with permission, unless it is an ordinary hiking tent.

Dogs must not be let loose from 1 March to 20 August — a month longer than the national lead period. Cycling, organised dog sledding and organised riding are allowed only on roads, routes or areas designated in the management plan, and e-bikes count as motor traffic. Motor traffic on land and water, and aircraft below 300 metres, is forbidden, as are motor-driven ice drills, model aircraft and model boats; under Miljødirektoratet's rule, drones may not take off in a national park or be flown into one without the park board's permission.

Organised activities that could harm the environment need permission from the Rondane-Dovre national park board. The reindeer are the reason the park exists: if you meet a herd, stop, keep your distance and let them move on, especially in the calving season and in winter.

From the south, via Grimsdalen and Grimsdalshytta

planYourVisit.reservations: No booking or fee. The park has little in the way of facilities: one marked path, also staked for skiers around Easter.
permits: Organised activities that could harm the environment need permission from the national park board
Flying a drone needs the national park board's permission; motor traffic is otherwise banned apart from the regulation's narrow exemptions
camping: Wild camping under the right to roam; a tent may stay more than a week in one place only with permission, unless it is an ordinary hiking tent
lodging: Grimsdalshytta, the Norwegian Trekking Association's lodge at the park's south-eastern edge

chronology.text: Wild reindeer are roaming these mountains after the ice retreats.
Hunters build trapping systems of guiding fences, pits and bow emplacements across the fells.
Pilgrims bound for St Olav's shrine in Nidaros cross Dovre on the main road between eastern Norway and Trøndelag.
Rondane becomes Norway's first national park; Dovre, created later, protects the range of the same reindeer herd.
The pilgrim route between Oslo and Nidaros is marked and reopened.
Dovre National Park is created on 24 October, joining Rondane and Dovrefjell-Sunndalsfjella into one protected reindeer range.

safety: The plateaus are exposed and featureless in fog and snow. Carry map and compass, and turn back early in bad weather.
There is only one marked path. Plan routes off it with care, and allow for wet ground in the mires and kettle holes.
Keep well clear of reindeer; a disturbed herd can abandon its grazing or its calves.
regulations: Dogs may not run loose from 1 March to 20 August.
No motor traffic or aircraft below 300 metres; no motor-driven model aircraft, model boats or ice drills, and no drones without the park board's permission.
Cycling and organised dog sledding or riding only on designated routes; e-bikes count as motor traffic.
No open fires in or near forest from 15 April to 15 September unless the municipality allows it.

weather: This is high, open mountain country, almost all of it above the tree line and parts of it nearly arctic. Summer is short and changeable on the plateaus; snow can fall in any month. The marked route through the park is staked for skiers around Easter, when the days are long and the snow settled. Autumn is the season for small-game and reindeer hunting.
directions: The Dovre Line between Oslo and Trondheim stops at Dombås, west of the park, and at Hjerkinn, to the north; the E6 follows the same route over Dovrefjell. The southern side is reached by road through Grimsdalen to Grimsdalshytta.
